description: PulseNova is a solo project for the "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts" challenge. We are building an AI health monitor that tracks heart rate, sleep, body temperature and mood, uses machine learning to spot unusual patterns, and gives colour-coded status with simple, plain-language guidance. Built with Python and Streamlit.
summary: PulseNova is a prototype health monitor for astronauts on space missions. The astronaut enters four daily readings: heart rate, sleep, body temperature and mood. The app shows each reading as green, yellow or red, draws charts over time, and explains in plain English what each reading means in space. A small machine-learning model spots unusual days, simple health rules decide which ones are worrying, and an AI assistant explains them in a few sentences and says when to contact the flight surgeon. It also has a friendly chat and a body view. It addresses the challenge by gathering health indicators and helping astronauts evaluate and act on them. This matters because on long missions astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting health changes in themselves. All data in the demo is simulated. It is a prototype, not medical advice.
details:
THE PROBLEM In deep space an astronaut cannot always reach a doctor quickly, so they need to understand their own health data. The challenge asks for software that gathers health indicators and helps astronauts evaluate and act on their health.

WHAT PULSENOVA DOES

  • Input form and dashboard (Streamlit): the astronaut types in four readings. The app checks them (empty or impossible values are rejected) and shows each as green, yellow or red with a large, clear label. Charts show how each reading changes over time.
  • Simple explanations: each reading has a short plain-English note about what it is and why it matters in space.
  • Finding unusual days: an Isolation Forest model (scikit-learn) looks at 180 days of readings and flags days that look unusual.
  • Health rules: unusual is not always unhealthy (for example, 8.5 hours of sleep). So a rule layer, with limits taken from public health sources (MedlinePlus and Cleveland Clinic), keeps only days with an unhealthy reading. Status is the worst of the four readings.
  • AI explanation: for flagged days, the Gemini API writes a short, plain explanation and one general wellness suggestion. On red days it says to contact the flight surgeon. It must use only numbers from the readings, and the app checks this.
  • Body view: a simple body drawing coloured by status (heart, brain, thermometer, moon) with buttons to read each explanation.
  • Chat: a small round astronaut button opens a friendly chat that already knows today's readings. It gives general wellness help only, never names medicines, and never diagnoses. Chest pain or distress messages always get a message to contact the flight surgeon and a crew member. The app also removes emails and phone numbers before sending a message.

HOW WE CHECKED IT The simulated data has 14 hidden problem days (fever, poor sleep, high heart rate, low mood). The model alone caught all 14 (recall 1.00) but had 9 false alarms (precision 0.61). With the health rules, precision rose to 0.88 with recall still 1.00. Honest limit: the rules alone score almost the same on this simulated data, so the model would matter more with real, subtler data. The project has more than 140 automated tests.

SAFETY AND HONESTY All data is simulated. The app is a prototype, not a medical device, and gives only general wellness information.

TOOLS Python, Streamlit, scikit-learn, pandas, NumPy, joblib, Google Gemini API, pytest, ruff.

HOW SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) WAS USED

  • To build the project: Claude (Anthropic) helped with planning, and Claude Code helped write and test the code in small steps. Claude also helped make the 7-slide demo deck, the team logo and the body and astronaut drawings. Duaa Javed wrote the instructions, chose the design (indicators, rules, chat behaviour), approved every change to the AI prompts, ran the app herself and took every screenshot. The full list of prompts and what was checked or changed is in prompt_log.md in the GitHub repository.
  • Inside the app: the Gemini API (Google) writes the explanations and chat answers, guided by a fixed system prompt with safety rules. The app adds its own safety checks in code, so safety does not depend on the AI alone.
  • AI-generated code and text were tested and read before use. Health limits come from public sources, not from the AI.

FUTURE WORK Use real mission data, add blood pressure and blood sugar, personal baselines for each astronaut, more languages, and review by a flight surgeon.
